headline.title: Our south pole maps vs NASA illumination and Earth visibility maps

source.label: NASA PGDA, south pole illumination products

headline.note: 20 points with x, y uniform and r <= 150 km (seed 42), each with its own horizon (LOLA polar 40 m + 120 m, observer at 2 m); 'any part of the disc', 54384 hourly steps (one in three) from 2026-01-01 over 18.6 years. NASA: mean of 3 x 3 pixels of the 60 m maps (terrain up to 2013, surface observer); bias Sun +0.8, Earth +1.0 points. Our 18.6-year mean with the any-part-of-the-disc criterion (one hourly step in three from 2026-01-01, observer 2 m above the terrain, LOLA 40 m + 120 m terrain with data to 2017) against NASA AVGVISIB (any part of the disc, hourly, 18.6 years, ground level, LOLA 60 m terrain with data to 2013). NASA values are 3 x 3 pixel means at each 500 m cell centre: the 60 m maps (85° S, up to 151.7 km from the pole) and, beyond them, the 120 m maps. The 2 m observer makes our values slightly higher.

cases.title: Sunset seen by Blue Ghost 1 (16 March 2025)
cases.expected: Sunset between 18:00 and 18:15 UTC (last data 23:15 UTC, 5 hours into the lunar night)

source.label: Firefly Aerospace, end of Blue Ghost Mission 1 surface operations

cases.obtained: Sun starts to set 18:20 UTC, centre on the horizon 18:54 UTC, fully set 19:28 UTC
cases.note: Retired (decision D-95): the check was badly posed, not failed. Firefly published no sunset time, only that the final data arrived around 23:15 UTC, "just over 5 hours into the lunar night"; the 18:00-18:15 UTC window was our own deduction. With real terrain (SLDEM2015, observer 2 m) our model has the Sun start to set at 18:20 UTC, its centre on the horizon at 18:54 UTC and fully set at 19:28 UTC, against 20:11 UTC on a smooth Moon. The horizon there is an 11 m rise 800 m away: moving the site by one terrain pixel (59 m) moves the sunset by up to 51 minutes, more than any useful tolerance. The model is unchanged.
